items.q: HTTP is described as 'stateless.' What does that mean for security?
options: Each request arrives on its own; the server doesn't remember you between requests unless something (like a session) carries that
The server remembers every user automatically, so no extra work is needed
Data sent over HTTP can't be changed in transit

explain.right: HTTP forgets between requests, so apps add sessions to remember you — and the server must treat every incoming request as independent and untrusted.
explain.wrong: It doesn't remember automatically, says nothing about tamper-protection (that's TLS), and isn't about connection stability.

items.q: Your form has JavaScript that blocks invalid input in the browser. Is server-side validation still needed?
options: No — the browser already blocked bad input
Only if the form handles passwords
Yes — anything the client sends is attacker-controllable, so the server must validate too
No — as long as the site uses HTTPS

explain.right: Client-side checks are a convenience; an attacker bypasses the browser and sends requests directly, so the server must always validate.
explain.wrong: Browser checks and HTTPS don't stop a hand-crafted request, and this applies to all input, not just passwords.

items.q: An attacker steals a user's session cookie. What can they do?
options: Nothing, unless they also know the password
Change the user's password remotely with no other access
Act as that logged-in user until the session expires, without knowing the password
Only read the cookie's name, not use it

explain.right: The session cookie is a temporary key to the account; whoever holds it is 'logged in' as that user — this is session hijacking.
explain.wrong: They don't need the password, the cookie is usable not just readable, and what they can do depends on being that user, not an automatic password reset.

items.q: A site shows the padlock / uses HTTPS. Which conclusion is CORRECT?
options: The data between your browser and that server is encrypted and tamper-protected in transit — but the site could still be a scam or full of bugs
The site's stored data is automatically encrypted too
The site is safe and trustworthy

explain.right: HTTPS protects confidentiality and integrity in transit and verifies the domain's certificate — nothing more. Phishing sites get valid certs easily.
explain.wrong: HTTPS does not make a site honest, bug-free, audited, or its stored data encrypted; that's the classic 'padlock = safe' misconception.

items.q: In one or two sentences: what does HTTPS protect, and name one thing it does NOT protect?
rubric: States HTTPS protects data in transit (confidentiality + integrity between browser and server)
Mentions it verifies the server's domain/certificate (optional but good)
Names something out of scope: stored data, access control, input validation, or site trustworthiness

explain.right: Good answers scope HTTPS to the transit pipe and name an out-of-scope concern like stored data or whether the site is trustworthy.
explain.wrong: A weak answer says 'HTTPS makes the site secure,' which overclaims what encryption in transit does.
